title: The name on the meat
hookLine: the animal is killed swiftly, with Allah's name, a sharp blade, and mercy
last: NIKAH — A FEELING ISN'T A SIN.

lines: NOT JUST WHICH ANIMAL, BUT HOW.
cards: Supermarket meat arrives on a foam tray under plastic, and the moment the animal died is somebody else's business. Islam doesn't let that moment disappear. Halal meat isn't just about which animals.
It's about how. There's a name that has to be said, and a blade that has to be sharp. And a hadith puts one word over the whole thing, a word you wouldn't expect at a slaughterhouse.

teach.h: DHABIHAH — THE NAME AND THE CUT.
teach.b: The word is dhabihah, an animal slaughtered in the prescribed way. The core is simple. The one slaughtering says the name of Allah, usually bismillah, Allahu akbar.
Then one swift cut across the throat with a very sharp blade, so it's over quickly and the blood drains out, since the Qur'an forbids eating blood.

teach.h: EAT WHAT HIS NAME WAS SAID OVER.
teach.b: The name comes from the Qur'an: in Surah al-An'am, believers are told to eat of what Allah's name has been said over, and not of what it hasn't.
Some teachers explain the name as a reminder that the life being taken was never ours: it's taken with permission, not by right. Then the word.

Sahih Muslim reports, from Shaddad ibn Aws, that the Prophet ﷺ said: Allah has written ihsan on everything. Ihsan means excellence, beauty, doing a thing as well as it can be done. So when you slaughter, slaughter well.
Let each of you sharpen his blade, and spare the animal suffering. Other reports go further: don't sharpen the knife where the animal can see, and don't slaughter one animal in front of another.
The same collections tell of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog, and a woman punished for starving a cat. Mercy even here, at the hardest moment.

Muslims differ on some modern questions: scholars disagree about stunning before slaughter, and about whether ordinary meat from Jews and Christians, whose food the Qur'an calls lawful, still counts today.
Under the debates sit the plain basics: say the name, keep the blade sharp, and be kind.

how: Halal meat comes from an animal slaughtered with Allah's name spoken, one swift cut with a sharp blade, the blood drained, and care to spare it suffering; Muslims also say bismillah before eating.

o: any meat a Muslim has blessed before eating
meat from animals that were raised on grass
meat slaughtered with God's name and a swift cut

games.q: what's inside dhabihah — tap the pairs.
p: sharpened, out of the animal's sight

s: halal is only about which animals may be eaten
it's also how: the name, one swift cut, and sparing the animal suffering.
a hadith says Allah has written ihsan, excellence, on everything, even slaughter
so when you slaughter, slaughter well; sharpen the blade (Muslim, from Shaddad ibn Aws).
all scholars agree about stunning before slaughter
scholars differ about stunning, and about meat from Jews and Christians today.

games.q: you're about to slaughter a sheep for a family meal. the knife is a little dull. what does the hadith say?
o: dull is fine, just work harder
sharpen your blade and spare the animal suffering
games.why: let each of you sharpen his blade and spare his animal suffering (Muslim 1955). mercy even at the hardest moment.

practice: Bukhari reports that the Prophet told a young boy at his table: say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you. So picture your next meal, and pause before the first bite.

If you pray, you can say bismillah, in the name of Allah; if not, remember that something, a plant or an animal, went into this plate, and someone grew it, caught it or cooked it, and give one breath of thanks.

wordCard.voice: Dhabihah. Meat slaughtered in the prescribed way: Allah's name, a swift cut with a sharp blade, and mercy. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: an animal slaughtered in the prescribed way, from dhabaha, to slaughter.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy even here. Ihsan is written on everything, even this. Day one hundred forty-five, done.

sources.ref: Qur'an 6:118, 6:121 (eat what Allah's name was said over)
Qur'an 5:5 (the food of the People of the Book)
Sahih Muslim 1955 (Shaddad ibn Aws: ihsan in everything)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5376 (say the name of Allah and eat with your right hand)
